articles.title: First President To Attend Law School… Also Hated It
articles.content:
Rutherford B. Hayes is the first U.S. president to get a law degree, but not the first one to attend a law school. Who was the first president to attend law school… before dropping out?

Hint: Despite never graduating, he was ultimately admitted to the bar and there’s a law school named after him today.

See the answer on the next page.

articles.title: How You Can Grow Your Firm Without Burning Out Its Professionals
articles.content:
In a recent conversation with Scott Rahn, Founding Partner of RMO Lawyers, I explored a question every growing firm eventually faces: How do you keep growing without sacrificing the people and the reputation that got you there?
Scott brings the perspective of a leader who has built a high-stakes trust, estate, and probate litigation practice through steady growth — and who has learned along the way that culture is protected or lost one decision at a time.
It All Starts With Hiring
When Steve asked what tips Scott could offer leaders trying to build a firm, regardless of generation, Scott didn’t hesitate. The single most important role a leader plays is in the hiring process: screening for, and ultimately hiring, the right people.
How a Scarcity Mindset Fuels Burnout
Scott described how a scarcity mindset can turn into something close to greed out of fear. Firms overcommit themselves, their teams, and their clients. When they can’t deliver, the first thing to suffer is their reputation. Worse, they end up burning out their teams and losing their best people.
The Top 3 Qualities in a New Hire
The biggest paycheck is not always the best career move. If the culture, values, and environment do not fit, you may be job hunting again in six months. This goes for employers as well as employees.
.
Steve Fretzin is a five-time bestselling author, host of the BE THAT LAWYER and Future Rainmakers podcasts, and a business development coach who works exclusively with attorneys. For more than 18 years, he has helped lawyers build strong books of business without selling, pitching, or chasing, using his proven Sales-Free Selling™ approach. His clients consistently become top rainmakers and credit his coaching and systems for driving meaningful, measurable growth. Steve can be reached directly at steve@fretzin.com, or through his website at bethatlawyer.com. Connect with him on LinkedIn at https://www.linkedin.com/in/stevefretzin. His ALL NEW BE THAT LAWYER Community is changing how lawyers develop the skills never taught in law school. Learn more at bethatlawyer.com/community.
The post How You Can Grow Your Firm Without Burning Out Its Professionals appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: How Appealing Weekly Roundup
articles.content:
Ed. note: A weekly roundup of just a few items from Howard Bashman’s How Appealing blog, the Web’s first blog devoted to appellate litigation. Check out these stories and more at How Appealing.
“Trump Lawyer Urges Appeals Court to Toss Hush-Money Case”: Patricia Hurtado and David Voreacos of Bloomberg News have this report.
“Alito and Thomas Can’t Retire Now; Such a nakedly political move would undercut any effort to preserve the high court’s independence”: Columnist James Taranto has this essay online at The Wall Street Journal.
“The looming constitutional showdowns — Investigations, the electoral college, the Supreme Court and pardons: The GOP collapse brings new volatility.” Columnist Jason Willick has this essay online at The Washington Post.
“Newsom commutes all 548 California death sentences in historic move”: Hannah Wiley, Sophia Bollag, and Bob Egelko of The San Francisco Chronicle have this report.
“Why a Merciless Supreme Court Rebuke on Election Eve Matters; The justices took just hours to reject Trump’s bid to meddle in the election”: Adam Liptak has this new installment of his “The Docket” newsletter online at The New York Times.
The post How Appealing Weekly Roundup appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Subpoenas Are Coming: Washington Law Firms Are Getting Ready For A Congressional Probe Boom
articles.content:
Ed. note: Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day.
Congressional investigations will be the busiest area of law in Washington over the next two years.
— Brian Nieves, a partner at Holtzman Vogel and former deputy counsel to the House Oversight Committee, in comments to Reuters. Democrats’ victories in both chambers mean they’ll take control of Congress, and gain subpoena power, in January. They’ve already signaled plans to investigate the Trump administration, its allies, and companies that did business with them. “Bottom line, there will be more investigators and more investigations,” said Mark Epley, who co-leads Arnold & Porter’s congressional investigations practice. Cooley’s Susanne Sachsman Grooms warned the volume of probes could double. Among the potential targets: nine major law firms that collectively agreed to provide Trump $940 million in free legal services. House Oversight’s incoming Democratic chair, Rep. Robert Garcia, has already offered a succinct preview: “Lawyer up.”
Staci Zaretsky is the managing editor of Above the Law, where she’s worked since 2011. She’d love to hear from you, so please feel free to email her with any tips, questions, comments, or critiques. You can follow her on Bluesky, X/Twitter, and Threads, or connect with her on LinkedIn.
